strengths: Timely problem: evaluation for text-to-audio-video generation is underdeveloped, and the paper targets an important gap involving audio-video synchronization, instruction following, and realism beyond unimodal quality metrics.

The benchmark design is reasonably broad: 500 long, compositional prompts, a taxonomy covering visual, audio, and cross-modal factors, and evaluation of 11 systems including closed-source, open-source, and composed pipelines.

The paper provides useful diagnostic structure, including separate objective metrics, instruction-following checklists, and realism dimensions such as temporal continuity, object integrity, acoustic artifacts, and material-timbre consistency.
The results are potentially informative for the community, especially the observation that audio realism and material-timbre consistency lag behind visual realism in current systems.

Presentation is generally understandable, with clear tables for model comparisons and detailed appendix prompts/templates for the MLLM judge. The limitations section acknowledges MLLM bias and benchmark scale limits.
weaknesses: The central MLLM-as-a-judge evaluation is insufficiently validated. The paper does not report human agreement, inter-annotator reliability, calibration against human ratings, sensitivity to judge choice, or confidence intervals. Since many headline findings rely on Gemini-2.5-Pro judgments, this is a major soundness concern.

Claims of being the first or comprehensive benchmark are overstated given closely related T2AV benchmarks such as VABench, JavisBench, Verse-Bench, Harmony-Bench, and UniAVGen. The novelty over these works is not separated cleanly from scale, prompt complexity, and the choice of judge taxonomy.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper describes sources and templates but does not clearly commit to releasing the 500 prompts, generated outputs, code, model API settings, exact model versions, or all intermediate checklist annotations. Closed-source systems and proprietary Gemini judging further limit reproducibility.

The experimental protocol may be unfair or confounded: models are run at different resolutions, some pipelines receive Gemini-paraphrased prompts while others apparently do not, and native default settings are used despite large differences across services. These choices can materially affect video quality, instruction following, and audio alignment scores.

The objective metrics are assembled from existing tools but their suitability for generated T2AV is not analyzed deeply. For example, CLAP/ImageBind/VideoCLIP similarities and desynchronization metrics may miss fine-grained causal alignment, and the paper does not quantify metric reliability or failure cases.

Dataset construction details remain underspecified despite the appendix. The paper reports semantic diversity and complexity statistics, but does not give enough information about clustering choices, source distribution, human audit procedures, annotator expertise, or quality-control criteria to assess dataset bias and coverage.

The comparison with existing benchmarks is partly qualitative and based on table dimensions rather than empirical evidence that T2AV-Compass produces more reliable, discriminative, or human-aligned evaluations.

Ethics and data governance are underdeveloped. The benchmark uses YouTube UGC and community prompts, but the paper does not discuss consent, copyright/licensing, privacy, identifiable people, speech data handling, or potential harms from evaluating/encouraging realistic audiovisual generation.

Several results are interpreted strongly without statistical support. There are no error bars, significance tests, bootstrap intervals, or variance estimates across prompts/judge runs, making rank differences and conclusions such as specific bottlenecks less convincing.

Writing quality is adequate but has noticeable polish issues and occasional overclaiming. Some figures/tables are dense, references include many future/preprint systems, and the appendix says all prompts are presented but appears mainly to include prompt templates rather than the full benchmark content.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely gap: evaluation for text-to-audio-video generation, where unimodal video or audio metrics are clearly insufficient.

The benchmark taxonomy is reasonably broad, covering video quality, audio quality, cross-modal alignment, instruction following, and realism, with useful subdimensions such as material-timbre consistency and temporal coherence.
The paper evaluates a relatively wide set of systems, including closed-source, open-source, and composed pipelines, and the tables give a helpful high-level snapshot of current model behavior.
The appendix includes many of the prompts used for checklist generation and MLLM judging, which is helpful for understanding the intended evaluation protocol.
weaknesses: The central empirical claims are not sufficiently supported because the MLLM-as-judge protocol is not validated against human judgments. There is no human agreement study, no correlation with expert ratings, no calibration analysis, and no evidence that Gemini-2.5-Pro can reliably judge subtle audio realism, temporal synchronization, physical plausibility, or instruction following in generated videos.

Reproducibility is weak. The benchmark prompts, generated outputs, source videos, code, evaluator configurations, and model API settings are not clearly released or specified. Many evaluated systems are proprietary, and the paper gives insufficient details on sampling, seeds, number of generations per prompt, API versions, retry handling, or postprocessing.

The evaluation may be unfair or confounded. The authors paraphrase prompts with Gemini-2.5-Pro for Ovi-1.1 and composed pipelines but apparently not for all systems, which can change task difficulty and makes comparisons hard to interpret. Resolution also differs across systems, e.g. Kling at 1080p and Javis at 480p, affecting quality metrics.

The benchmark construction is under-validated. The paper claims semantic diversity and superior distinctiveness, but the diversity measures are only briefly described and rely on embedding retention/similarity without clear statistical treatment or evidence that the taxonomy covers realistic user needs better than existing benchmarks.

Objective metrics are not sufficiently justified. Metrics such as CLAP, ImageBind, VideoCLIP, DOVER++, LAION aesthetics, Synchformer, and LatentSync are adopted, but the paper does not analyze their reliability for generated T2AV content or their agreement with human perception. Several reported scores are difficult to interpret because scale normalization and uncertainty are absent.

The results are mostly descriptive. The main insight, an audio realism bottleneck, is plausible but not deeply substantiated beyond MLLM scores. There are no confidence intervals, significance tests, ablations of benchmark components, sensitivity analyses for the judge, or error taxonomies grounded in manual inspection.

Originality is limited relative to recent audio-video generation benchmarks such as JavisBench, VABench, Verse-Bench, Harmony-Bench, and related multimodal evaluation work. The contribution is mainly aggregation of prompts plus existing metrics plus MLLM judging, rather than a clearly new evaluation methodology.

Ethical and legal treatment is inadequate. The benchmark uses YouTube videos, community prompts, speech-containing clips, and proprietary model outputs, but licensing, consent, privacy, copyright, and redistribution constraints are not addressed in a meaningful way.

The limitations section is too narrow. It mentions computational overhead, MLLM bias, and long-tail coverage, but misses more serious limitations: lack of human validation, possible judge/model circularity from using Gemini for rewriting and judging, non-reproducibility of proprietary systems, dataset licensing, and metric reliability.

Presentation has several rough edges, including grammatical issues, inconsistent terminology, formatting artifacts, and unclear references to missing figures or sources, which reduce confidence in the care taken with the benchmark specification.

strengths: Timely and useful benchmark for text-to-audio-video generation, an area where evaluation is clearly underdeveloped relative to model progress.

The benchmark design is broader than many prior suites: 500 complex prompts, explicit coverage of video quality, audio quality, cross-modal alignment, instruction following, and realism, plus fine-grained audio/video subdimensions.

The paper evaluates a strong and practically relevant model set, including closed-source systems, open-source systems, and composed pipelines, yielding informative comparisons and actionable observations such as the audio realism bottleneck.

The taxonomy-driven prompt construction and video-inversion stream are sensible, and the appendices include many prompt templates and rubric definitions, which improves interpretability of the benchmark.

The results are diagnostically presented rather than only ranked: subdimension analyses expose specific weaknesses in dynamics, material-timbre consistency, audio artifacts, and instruction following.
weaknesses: The central evaluation relies heavily on Gemini-2.5-Pro as an MLLM judge, but the paper provides no convincing validation against human judgments, inter-annotator agreement, judge-model correlation, or ablation over different judges. This is the main soundness concern because the headline subjective results depend on an unvalidated evaluator.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The manuscript describes prompts and rubrics, but does not clearly commit to releasing the 500 prompts, generated outputs, source URLs/timestamps, code, model invocation settings, or judge outputs. Closed-source model APIs and changing model versions further reduce reproducibility.

Experimental fairness is imperfect: systems are evaluated at different native resolutions, some prompts are paraphrased with Gemini for specific pipelines, and generation settings are mostly left at vendor defaults. These choices may be practical, but they confound model comparisons and are not sufficiently analyzed.

The objective metrics are reasonable but mostly inherited proxies; the paper does not establish that they are reliable for complex T2AV outputs or that the proposed metric aggregation reflects human preference. Some metrics may also reward superficial semantic similarity rather than temporal or causal audiovisual grounding.

The dataset construction has several under-specified human steps: manual audits, human refinement, and human-in-the-loop verification are mentioned without annotator counts, expertise, guidelines, adjudication procedure, or quality-control statistics.

The novelty is primarily in benchmark integration and coverage rather than a fundamentally new evaluation methodology. Related benchmarks such as VABench and JavisBench appear close enough that the manuscript should more sharply substantiate what is uniquely enabled by T2AV-Compass.

Ethics and data governance are thin. The benchmark uses YouTube UGC and community prompts, but the paper does not discuss licensing, consent, privacy, takedown procedures, or whether videos containing people or speech are handled appropriately.

The presentation is generally understandable but has many polish issues, including formatting artifacts, awkward phrasing, inconsistent model names/capitalization, and some unclear table labels. These do not block understanding but weaken confidence in the benchmark documentation.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important gap: evaluating text-to-audio-video generation jointly rather than through loosely combined unimodal metrics. The proposed taxonomy spans video quality, audio quality, cross-modal alignment, instruction following, and realism, which is well matched to the failure modes of current T2AV systems.

The benchmark construction is more ambitious than many prior evaluations: 500 dense prompts, multiple prompt sources, a video-inversion stream grounded in real clips, deduplication, clustering/sampling, LLM rewriting, and human refinement. The prompts appear designed to stress compositionality, physical plausibility, audio events, and cinematographic constraints.

The evaluation covers a broad set of 15 systems, including proprietary end-to-end models, open-source models, and cascaded pipelines. This makes the empirical comparison useful and gives the benchmark practical diagnostic value.

The paper goes beyond leaderboard reporting. It includes fine-grained subdimension tables, difficulty analyses by subject/event complexity, metric-correlation analysis, human validation of AV synchronization, human-vs-MLLM agreement analysis, pairwise human preference validation, and robustness checks across repeated MLLM judging runs.

The limitations section is honest about MLLM bias, computational overhead, dependence on Gemini, version drift, and incomplete long-tail prompt coverage. The paper also explicitly treats MLLM judging as a scalable proxy rather than a bias-free oracle.
weaknesses: The central evaluation pipeline relies heavily on proprietary MLLM judges, especially Gemini-2.5-Pro, which weakens reproducibility and long-term stability. Vendor updates, hidden model changes, and closed model behavior could materially alter benchmark scores.

Human validation is helpful but still limited relative to the claims. The main human-vs-MLLM agreement analysis uses a 50-prompt subset across five models, while the benchmark conclusions are drawn from 500 prompts and 15 systems. Agreement is notably weak for audio realism: Gemini-2.5-Pro has L1 1.420 versus inter-human 1.042, which is a large gap for a dimension central to the paper's 'audio realism bottleneck' claim.

The paper combines many heterogeneous metrics, but the score normalization, aggregation choices, and statistical uncertainty are not always sufficiently justified. The overall averages in Table 3 may obscure calibration differences among dimensions, and the paper does not report confidence intervals or significance tests for many leaderboard differences.

Several objective metrics are inherited from prior models such as CLAP, ImageBind, Synchformer, DOVER++, and NISQA. These are reasonable choices, but the paper sometimes presents them as a stable basis for T2AV evaluation without fully probing known weaknesses, such as semantic embedding shortcuts, domain mismatch, and poor sensitivity to fine-grained audiovisual causality.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed. The manuscript states that code and data are available, but the visible text has an incomplete availability statement. Closed-source generators, security-review failures, and proprietary judges make exact reproduction difficult; the paper should report generation failure counts, API/version details, seeds/settings where applicable, and whether generated outputs will be released.

Dataset ethics and licensing are underdeveloped. The benchmark uses community prompts and YouTube clips for video inversion, but the manuscript gives little detail on licensing, consent, personally identifiable content handling, or whether generated dense captions from real videos preserve potentially sensitive information.

Originality is meaningful but moderate. The benchmark is broader than prior work and adds useful diagnostic structure, but much of the methodology is an integration of existing metrics, LLM-generated checklists, and MLLM-as-judge protocols. The paper's novelty rests mainly on coverage and careful taxonomy rather than a fundamentally new evaluation method.

Presentation is generally clear, but there are rough edges: some figures/tables appear hard to parse in the manuscript extraction, there are minor formatting issues, and some claims such as 'first comprehensive benchmark' are stronger than warranted given contemporaneous T2AV benchmarks like VABench and JavisBench.

strengths: The paper targets an important and timely gap: evaluation of text-to-audio-video generation across video quality, audio quality, cross-modal alignment, instruction following, and realism. A benchmark that jointly stresses audio, video, and synchronization would be useful to the community.

The proposed taxonomy is reasonably broad, covering visual attributes, dynamics, cinematography, aesthetics, relations, world knowledge, sound effects, speech, music, and realism dimensions such as temporal coherence and material-timbre consistency.

The paper evaluates a comparatively wide set of systems, including end-to-end, cascaded, open-source, and proprietary models, and the reported results surface plausible qualitative trends such as weak audio realism and degradation under long-narrative prompts.
The authors make some effort to validate automated judging, including human-MLLM agreement on a subset, pairwise human comparisons, repeated judge runs, and limited synchronization validation.
weaknesses: The central evaluation methodology is not sufficiently reliable. Much of the benchmark depends on Gemini-2.5-Pro as both prompt/checklist generator and judge, yet the human validation is small relative to the claimed 500-prompt benchmark and shows substantial disagreement, especially for audio realism. This directly weakens the paper's main claims about fine-grained model ranking and the alleged audio realism bottleneck.

Reproducibility is a major concern. The manuscript says code and data are available at a blank location and HuggingFace, but no actual link is provided. Many evaluated systems are closed-source or changing proprietary services, some generations failed due to security review, and the protocol relies on closed Gemini variants, making the headline leaderboard hard to reproduce or audit.

The benchmark construction is under-specified and potentially biased. Prompts are heavily rewritten by Gemini to add constraints, but the paper gives little evidence that these rewrites preserve original intent, remain physically plausible, or avoid stylistic/model-specific biases. Human refinement is mentioned but annotator counts, criteria, disagreement, and rejected-case analysis are not adequately reported.

The experimental comparison is not controlled enough. Models are run at different native resolutions and settings, and some pipelines receive Gemini-paraphrased prompts while others apparently receive the original benchmark prompts. This can confound conclusions about model capability with input adaptation and configuration differences.

Several objective metrics are adopted without enough validation for this setting. CLAP, VideoCLIP, ImageBind, DOVER, NISQA, Synchformer, and LatentSync each measure proxies that may not correspond to the paper's high-level claims; the manuscript reports many metrics but provides limited evidence that they are calibrated for complex T2AV prompts.

The presentation has notable quality issues for a main-track submission: duplicated or mislabeled figures, corrupted glyph extraction in figures, duplicate table numbering, awkward phrasing, missing repository links, and some inconsistent model/version naming. These problems reduce confidence in the care taken with the benchmark release.

The significance is limited by overlap with very recent related benchmarks such as VABench, JavisBench, Harmony-Bench, and Verse-Bench. The paper claims to be the first comprehensive benchmark, but the novelty over contemporaneous work is mostly broader taxonomy plus MLLM judging, which is not yet convincingly validated.

The ethics and data-use discussion is thin. The paper uses YouTube videos and community prompts but does not adequately discuss licensing, consent, personal data, potential copyright constraints, or how released benchmark assets will handle these issues. The misinformation risk statement is brief and generic.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely gap: evaluation for text-to-audio-video generation is less mature than T2V or T2A evaluation, and the proposed benchmark targets genuinely multimodal issues such as audio-video alignment, temporal synchronization, instruction following, and realism.

The benchmark construction is thoughtful. The 500 prompts are taxonomically curated, relatively dense, and supplemented with 100 real-video inversion prompts to improve physical plausibility; the paper also reports useful statistics on prompt length, semantic diversity, subject count, event structure, and audio composition.

The evaluation suite is broad and diagnostic rather than a single leaderboard score. It combines established objective metrics for video, audio, and cross-modal alignment with checklist-based MLLM judging for instruction following and perceptual realism.

The empirical study is useful and unusually comprehensive for this emerging task, covering 15 systems including closed-source frontier models, open-source models, and cascaded pipelines. The resulting analyses identify concrete bottlenecks, especially audio realism, sound-effect grounding, dynamics, and long-horizon event structure.

The authors make a serious attempt to validate the MLLM judge: they compare against human ratings on a 50-prompt/250-sample subset, include pairwise ranking validation via Bradley-Terry/Elo, report repeated-judge robustness, and discuss metric redundancy and preprocessing sensitivity.

The limitations section is candid about computational overhead, dependence on closed-source Gemini judges, judge bias, and limited long-tail coverage. This improves the credibility of the benchmark rather than weakening it.
weaknesses: The central evaluation still depends heavily on closed-source Gemini variants. Although the human agreement study is helpful, it is limited to 50 prompts and 5 systems, and audio realism agreement is notably worse than other dimensions, which weakens confidence in one of the paper's main bottleneck claims.

Reproducibility is only partially addressed. The paper says code/data will be released, but the manuscript does not provide enough concrete release details, version pinning for proprietary models/judges, or scripts/configuration specifics to fully reproduce the main leaderboard, especially for closed-source systems that may change over time.

The benchmark's originality is solid but not exceptional: many ingredients are adapted from existing benchmark practice, including prompt taxonomies, reference-free metrics, CLAP/ImageBind/VideoCLIP-style alignment, and MLLM-as-judge checklists. The contribution is mainly integration and careful benchmarking rather than a fundamentally new evaluation method.

Some methodological choices may affect fairness. Certain pipelines receive Gemini-2.5-Pro paraphrased prompts to better match their requirements, while others appear to use the original prompts; this could change prompt difficulty and complicate direct model comparisons.

The aggregate average score in Table 3 is convenient but somewhat arbitrary, since it combines heterogeneous dimensions without a clearly justified weighting scheme. The paper is strongest when interpreted dimension-wise, but the leaderboard framing may invite overinterpretation.

The dataset construction pipeline may introduce model and style biases because Gemini is used both to rewrite prompts and to generate dense captions/checklists, and Gemini is also the primary judge. This creates a possible evaluator-construction coupling that is not fully disentangled.

The paper would benefit from stronger statistical reporting: confidence intervals, bootstrap tests for leaderboard differences, and per-category sample counts would make it clearer which model gaps are robust versus noise.

The ethics discussion notes misinformation risks but is relatively brief on data provenance and rights, especially for YouTube-derived clips and community prompt sources. More detail on licensing, consent, filtering, and intended release conditions would improve the research-ethics treatment.
